LEQ-C.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the French Revolution changed the social structure of France between 1789 and 1815.
LEQ-C.scoringNotes: Accept as context: the Old Regime's three estates and the privileges of nobility and clergy, the fiscal crisis of the 1780s, Enlightenment criticism of privilege. Accept as evidence: abolition of feudal privileges August 1789, Declaration of the Rights of Man 1789, sale of Church lands, Civil Constitution of the Clergy 1790, abolition of noble titles 1790, the Terror, Napoleonic Code 1804, Concordat 1801, the new imperial nobility of 1808, careers open to talent, peasants keeping or gaining land, continued elite wealth, limited gains for women. Facts must be accurate to be credited.

DBQ-C.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which overseas trade and the arrival of American silver changed the economy of Western Europe between 1500 and 1650.
DBQ-C.scoringNotes: Accept as context: Portuguese and Spanish voyages after 1492, the decline of Mediterranean trade routes relative to Atlantic ports, the Spanish conquest of the Americas. Outside evidence examples: the Price Revolution, Potosi silver mines (1545), Spanish royal bankruptcies (1557, 1575, 1596), the Fuggers, Dutch East India Company (1602), Bank of Amsterdam (1609), English joint-stock companies, mercantilism, the putting-out system. Facts must be accurate to be credited. Document 5 describes guild weavers being undercut by merchants using cheaper rural labor.

sources.title: Document 1 - Report of a Castilian magistrate, about 1560 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: Since the fleets from the Indies began to arrive heavy with silver, everything in our market towns costs more than in my father's time. Bread, cloth and rents have all risen, yet the wages of day labourers have not kept pace, and many say they cannot feed their families. The merchants of Seville grow rich, and I fear for the order of the towns.

sources.title: Document 2 - Index of grain prices in Castile (1500 = 100) (ALTON-composed table)
Document 3 - Petition of Dutch merchants, 1602 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: We, merchants of several towns, humbly ask that our separate voyages to the Indies be joined in a single company with shares open to all citizens, so that the great costs and dangers may be borne by many hands and no man be ruined by the loss of one ship.

sources.title: Document 4 - English pamphlet on trade, 1620s (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: A kingdom grows rich when it sells more to strangers than it buys of them. Therefore foreign trade should be guarded by law, and the king should grant companies exclusive rights, so that the treasure of the realm is not carried abroad.

sources.title: Document 5 - Complaint of a guild master in a Flemish town, about 1580 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: Our weavers are ruined. The merchants of the port buy cloth made in the countryside, where wages are low and no guild rules bind them, and ship it overseas. The old rules of our guild are ignored and our members have no work.

sources.title: Document 6 - Letter from the Spanish Crown's finance office, 1627 (ALTON-composed)
sources.body: The silver that comes from the Indies is already promised to our creditors in Genoa and elsewhere. The Crown cannot pay its debts, and Spain's own makers of cloth cannot compete with the foreign goods that fill our markets, so the treasure leaves Spain almost as fast as it arrives.
